title: Modern Maths
tagline: P&C and probability — counting carefully beats formula-hunting.

subsections.title: Permutations & Combinations
subsections.trick: Ask ‘does order matter?’ before picking P or C — arrangements/rankings/passwords = P, selections/groups/committees = C. For circular arrangements, it's (n−1)!, not n! — fixing one position removes the rotational duplicates. Grid-path counting is really just ‘arrange m R's and n U's in a row’ — it's (m+n)Cm in disguise. If a question blocks off certain intersections, Pascal's-triangle-style running sums (add the count from the left neighbour and the neighbour below) survives even when the closed formula doesn't.

pyqs.q: How many R/U paths go from (0,0) to (4,4) on a grid?
pyqs.a: It's 8 moves total, 4 of each type — 8!/(4!4!) = ×70. Or build Pascal's triangle on the grid (each point = sum of the point to its left + the point below it) and read off (4,4): 1,4,10,20,×35,70 down the rows — works even if some cells were blocked.

pyqs.q: A cafeteria has 5 sandwich types, each customisable with 4 breads and 2 sizes. Find total distinct combinations.
pyqs.a: Independent choices multiply: 4 breads × 2 sizes = 8 options per sandwich type, and 5 types are separate menu items (not combined further), so total = 5×8 = ×40.

pyqs.q: (m+2n)(2m+n) = 27 for integers m,n. Find the maximum possible value of (2m−3n).
pyqs.a: 27 has only a few integer factor pairs: (1,27),(3,9),(9,3),(27,1) and their negatives. Test each pair as (m+2n, 2m+n), solve the resulting 2x2 linear system for integer m,n, and take the best (2m−3n) — works out to ×17.

subsections.title: Probability
subsections.trick: Mutually exclusive vs independent are different conditions — don't apply P(E)+P(F) when you actually need P(E)×P(F). Complement rule (1−P(E)) is usually faster than direct counting for ‘at least one’ questions.

formulas.label: Mutually exclusive events
formulas.latex: P(A\cap B) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; P(A \text{ or } B) = P(A)+P(B)

formulas.label: Binomial probability (exactly k successes in n trials)

pyqs.q: Three fair coins are tossed. Find P(at least 2 heads).
pyqs.a: Binomial shortcut: P(X≥2) = C(3,2)(½)²(½)¹ + C(3,3)(½)³ = ³⁄₈+₁⁄₈ = ⁴⁄₈ = ×½. Scales cleanly to 5 or 6 coins where listing outcomes by hand gets painful.

subsections.title: Set Theory & Venn Diagrams
subsections.trick: When a question asks for a maximum or minimum count under overlap constraints, draw the 3-circle Venn and push values to the boundary allowed by the constraints — CAT set questions are almost always optimisation problems in disguise, not direct counting.

formulas.label: Three-set union
formulas.latex: |A\cup B\cup C| = |A|+|B|+|C|-|A\cap B|-|B\cap C|-|C\cap A|+|A\cap B\cap C|

pyqs.q: Students pick Physics, Chemistry, Maths. |P∩C| = |C∩M| = ½|P∩M|. Find the max possible number who chose Physics but not Maths.
pyqs.a: Push every overlap to its boundary value permitted by the |P∩C|=|C∩M|=½|P∩M| constraint, then maximise the 'Physics only + Physics∩Chemistry only' region while keeping Physics∩Maths as small as the constraint allows — gives ×55 students.
